name: The stages of economic growth

thinkers.name: W. W. Rostow
thinkers.note: American economic historian, later National Security Advisor to Lyndon Johnson and among the most committed advocates of the war in Vietnam. The two facts belong together: the book's subtitle is A Non-Communist Manifesto.

claim: Every society passes through the same five stages on the way to a modern economy, and the one that matters is a short take-off in which investment roughly doubles as a share of national income.
summary: Rostow's argument is that economic history has a shape, that the shape is the same everywhere, and that a country can be located on it. Five stages: traditional society, the preconditions for take-off, the take-off itself, the drive to maturity, and the age of high mass consumption. The take-off is the hinge. Rostow set three conditions for it, and the first is a number: net investment rises from around five per cent of national income to over ten.

The appeal to a planner is obvious. If the sequence is universal, then a poor country is not a different kind of thing from a rich one, only an earlier version of it, and the task is to supply the missing ingredient. That ingredient is capital. Aid, in this account, is not charity; it is the push that gets a country over the investment threshold, after which growth becomes self-sustaining.

The subtitle is doing work. Rostow wrote in 1960 against a Marxist account of history that also had stages, also claimed universality, and also promised industrialisation. He was offering the same promise without the revolution, and he was offering it to governments deciding which side of the Cold War to stand on. The theory travelled inside American foreign policy because it was built to.

axis_notes.allocation: Rostow assumes a mixed economy and is not doctrinaire about ownership, but the growth comes from private investment in leading sectors, with the state supplying the framework.
axis_notes.priority: As far towards grow-first as the shelf goes. Mass consumption is stage five; distribution is what a mature economy can afford, not a route to maturity.
axis_notes.hierarchy: Caste, race and gender are absent from the model. Traditional society is characterised by its production function, not by who is allowed to own or learn.
axis_notes.agency: The agents are a new elite, a centralising state and the entrepreneurs of the leading sector. Nothing in the sequence requires anybody poor to organise.

layers.title: A ceiling, not a floor
layers.text: Rostow's traditional society is not defined by poverty but by a limit. Pre-Newtonian science and technology mean the production function has a ceiling: output per head cannot rise past a certain point however hard anyone works, so most of the workforce stays in agriculture and the surplus goes to landowners who spend it on consumption rather than investment.

layers.title: Something arrives from outside
layers.text: The preconditions stage begins when the ceiling is disturbed, usually from outside: new ideas about the physical world, trade with a more advanced economy, or colonial intrusion. Rostow is explicit that for most of the world other than Britain the shock was external. A new elite forms that is willing to reinvest rather than consume, and a centralised state emerges that can build roads, ports and schools.

layers.title: The take-off, and its number
layers.text: Two or three decades in which growth becomes normal rather than exceptional. Rostow gives three conditions. Net investment rises from about five per cent of national income to over ten. One or more manufacturing sectors grow fast enough to pull others along behind them. And a political and institutional setting exists, or appears quickly, that lets the expansion continue. The investment figure is the part everyone remembers, and the part that made the theory operational for aid agencies.

layers.title: Growth spreads sideways
layers.text: The drive to maturity is the long stretch, around sixty years in Rostow's reckoning, in which modern technology stops being confined to the leading sector and reaches the rest of the economy. The country becomes able to produce not everything, but anything it chooses to produce. The composition of the workforce shifts out of agriculture and the leading sector of the take-off is overtaken by newer ones.

layers.title: What maturity is for
layers.text: At the final stage a society has a surplus beyond what production requires, and has to decide what to do with it. Rostow names three options that a mature economy chooses between: external power and influence, a welfare state, or private consumption of durable goods and services. The United States of the 1950s, with suburbs and cars, is the illustration. The stage is where the promise sits: this is what the sequence is for.

layers.title: The policy conclusion
layers.text: If the constraint on a poor country is the investment rate, then transferring capital into it moves it along the sequence. Aid becomes a temporary push with a defined end, and the country that receives it arrives at mass consumption without passing through a revolution. That inference, more than the historical scheme, is what carried the book into American development policy in the 1960s.

evidence.claim: Take-off shows up in the data as a sharp rise in the investment rate.
evidence.finding: Simon Kuznets went looking for the discontinuity in the historical national accounts and did not find it. Capital formation rose gradually in the countries Rostow cited rather than roughly doubling over two decades, and the dates Rostow assigned to each country's take-off did not line up with the dates the investment series suggested.
evidence.source: Simon Kuznets, 'Notes on the Take-Off', in W. W. Rostow (ed.), The Economics of Take-Off into Sustained Growth

evidence.claim: Latecomers repeat the path the first industrialisers took.
evidence.finding: Alexander Gerschenkron's comparative work on Europe found the opposite pattern: the later a country industrialised, the more it substituted for what it lacked. Britain financed industry from retained profits, Germany used investment banks, Russia used the state budget. The sequence was not repeated; it was replaced.
evidence.source: Alexander Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective

evidence.claim: Raising the investment rate is sufficient for sustained growth.
evidence.finding: India ran the experiment. Gross domestic saving and investment rose substantially across the plan decades while growth per head stayed near one and a half per cent a year into the 1970s, a rate slow enough to acquire a nickname. Capital went in; growth did not follow at the rate the model implied.
evidence.source: Raj Krishna's phrase 'the Hindu rate of growth' dates from 1978; the underlying series are in the Reserve Bank of India's national accounts

unsettled: The model has not been rescued, but neither has the question it asked been answered. Something does change when a country's growth becomes self-sustaining, and Rostow was asking about it in a form that could be tested, which is more than can be said for most of what surrounded him. What the evidence rules out is the specific mechanism, the universal sequence and the timetable. What it leaves open is whether there is any threshold at all, and the growth-diagnostics literature that replaced stage theory is still arguing about it.
india: Rostow's arithmetic and the Second Five Year Plan's arithmetic point the same way and come from different places. The Plan's target of lifting the savings rate is the take-off condition in all but name, and Indian planners of the 1950s read Rostow. But the Mahalanobis model that actually shaped the Plan is a different machine, concerned with the composition of investment rather than its level, and it prescribed heavy industry for reasons Rostow's leading-sector argument does not supply.
compare_note: Both make capital accumulation the engine and the state the organiser. Mahalanobis asks where the investment should go; Rostow only asks how much of it there is.
contrast_note: Rostow's external shock is what starts development. For dependency theory the same contact is what prevents it.
